kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க ஒருவன்தன் நெஞ்சத்து
அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkaaraak kolga oruvanthan nenjathu
Azhukkaaru ilaadha iyalbu.
kurals.meaning: Let a person adopt, as the very rule of their conduct, a nature whose heart holds no envy.
kurals.elementary: Some families have house rules, like “always say please.” This kural says: make “never be jealous of anyone” one of your own rules, as important as any other rule for being good.
kurals.university: Valluvar builds the chapter on a pun: ஒழுக்காறு (ozhukkaaru, “the path of right conduct”) and அழுக்காறு (azhukkaaru, “the path of impurity,” i.e., envy) differ by a single sound, so the couplet sets the right road against the soiled road. He places the absence of envy inside the heart (நெஞ்சத்து), not just in outward behavior, which treats envy as a flaw of character rather than a wrong act. Commentators from Parimelazhagar to Mu. Varadarasanar read the couplet as saying freedom from envy should be held as seriously as the formal rules of ozhukkam (Chapter 14). The view is close to Aristotle's, who counted envy among the passions whose very names imply badness, and to the Buddhist idea that a disposition must be trained, not merely a deed avoided.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but who is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor, who is free from false ego and equal both in happiness and distress, who is always satisfied and engaged in devotional service with determination and whose mind and intelligence are in agreement with Me-he is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the character traits of the ideal devotee, and “not envious” (adveṣṭā) comes first.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make freedom from envy a settled trait of character, the foundation of a good life rather than one rule among many.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel in placing non-envy first among virtues. Prabhupada renders adveṣṭā as “not envious”; other translators give “without hatred,” so the envy sense depends on this translation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul closes his list of the “fruit of the Spirit” by telling the community that people who live by the Spirit should not envy each other.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul makes not envying a standing rule of conduct for anyone who wants to live rightly.
christianity._accuracy_note: Direct command against envy framed as a norm of conduct; the Kural's pun on ozhukkaaru has no equivalent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not hate one another, and do not be jealous of one another, and do not desert each other, and O, Allah's worshipers! Be brothers.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists envy (tahāsud) among the things believers must never do to each other if they are to live as brothers.
islam.tie_back: Both texts turn “do not envy” into a basic rule of how a good person relates to others.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct prohibition of envy within a code of conduct; Sunnah.com (Muhsin Khan) translates tahāsud as “jealous.”

judaism.quote_or_event: “A good eye, a humble spirit and a moderate appetite he is of the disciples of Abraham, our father. An evil eye, a haughty spirit and a limitless appetite he is of the disciples of Balaam, the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah marks the followers of Abraham by a “good eye” (ayin tovah), a generous way of seeing others' good, and the followers of Balaam by an “evil eye,” a grudging one.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Avot treats a heart without envy as the sign of a whole way of life.
judaism._accuracy_note: “Evil eye” in rabbinic usage covers envy and stinginess; strong parallel in treating the trait as a mark of character.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Asked why beings who wish to live without hostility still live in hostility, the Buddha answers that devas, humans, and all other beings “are fettered with envy & stinginess.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Sakka-pañha Sutta, envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) are named as the two fetters behind all conflict between beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see envy as a basic flaw of the heart that must be removed for a good life, not a minor fault.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 21 (Sakka-pañha Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase with a short verbatim phrase from the Access to Insight translation. The sutta diagnoses rather than prescribes a rule of conduct.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says there are two Strifes on earth: one “a man would praise,” which spurs neighbour to compete with neighbour in honest work, and one that is “blameworthy,” fostering war and cruelty.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet separates healthy rivalry, which pushes a person to work harder, from the destructive strife that wants only to harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar's choice between the “right path” and the “impure path” matches Hesiod's choice between the good Strife and the bad one.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase with short verbatim phrases. Hesiod contrasts two forms of rivalry rather than naming envy as a character flaw, so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is therefore a good feeling felt by good persons, whereas envy is a bad feeling felt by bad persons.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle compares emulation (wanting to earn what another has) with envy (wanting the other not to have it), and calls envy a mark of a bad character.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Aristotle treats the presence or absence of envy as a test of the kind of person one is.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified in the MIT Internet Classics Archive text. Close conceptual match: envy is a matter of character.

kurals.tamil:
விழுப்பேற்றின் அஃதொப்பது இல்லையார் மாட்டும்
அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vizhuppetrin aqdhoppadhu illaiyaar maattum
Azhukkaatrin anmai perin.
kurals.meaning: If a person can be free of envy toward everyone, no other excellent gain they could ever obtain is equal to it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a treasure chest full of prizes: gold, trophies, toys. This kural says the best prize is a heart that is never jealous of anyone. Better than all the rest.
kurals.university: The key phrase is யார் மாட்டும் (“toward anyone at all”): Valluvar asks for complete freedom from envy, not selective freedom. Envy usually targets equals, as Aristotle observed, so envying no one means refusing to compare one's own standing with others'. By calling this the highest of all விழுப்பேறு (excellent attainments), the couplet puts an inner state above wealth, fame, and learning. The point anticipates the Stoic claim that goods in our control are the only true goods, and that once we see this, “there will be no room for envy.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is satisfied with gain which comes of its own accord, who is free from duality and does not envy, who is steady both in success and failure, is never entangled, although performing actions.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the free person as vimatsara, one without envy, content with whatever comes and steady in both success and failure.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts present freedom from envy as a supreme attainment that frees a person from bondage.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Vimatsara is a direct term for “free of envy”; the Gita does not rank it explicitly as the highest gain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,”
christianity.explanation: In the hymn to love, Paul says love “envieth not,” and closes the chapter by calling love the greatest of the three abiding gifts (13:13).
christianity.tie_back: The Kural calls an envy-free heart the greatest attainment; Paul makes the love that “envieth not” the greatest gift.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel via 13:13, although Paul ranks love, of which non-envy is one feature, rather than non-envy itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes complete faith depend on wanting for others the same good one wants for oneself, which is the opposite of envy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat a heart that wishes others well, without envy, as the highest attainment of the religious life.
islam._accuracy_note: Positive formulation of anti-envy. The Kural speaks of attainment; the hadith speaks of faith's completeness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment with one's own portion, not comparison with others.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts put a heart that does not measure itself against others above any outward prize.
judaism._accuracy_note: Contentment is the positive side of non-envy; the mishnah does not mention envy explicitly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A monk who does not despise what he has received, even though it be little, who is pure in livelihood and unremitting in effort — him even the gods praise.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse after the warning against envying others' gains (Dhp 365) praises the monk who is content with his own.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts rank contentment free from envy as an attainment worth more than material gain.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Read with verse 365, which explicitly condemns envy; verse 366 alone speaks of contentment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple in Phrygia, share their meager meal with disguised gods whom richer neighbours turned away; they are rewarded while the neighbourhood is drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple are content with their humble lot and give freely, with no resentment of wealthier neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their contentment, free of envy, turns out to be worth more than their neighbours' wealth, echoing the Kural's ranking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: the story centers on hospitality and piety; freedom from envy is implied, not stated.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For, if the essence of good consists in things in our own control, there will be no room for envy or emulation.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus says that once you see real goods as inner ones, no one else's honors or power can make you envious. The only thing worth wanting is to be free.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers see freedom from envy as the sign of the highest good a person can reach.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on MIT Internet Classics Archive. Epictetus derives non-envy from true goods rather than ranking it as the top good.

kurals.tamil:
அறன்ஆக்கம் வேண்டாதான் என்பான் பிறனாக்கம்
பேணாது அழுக்கறுப் பான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aran aakkam vendaadhaan enbaan piranaakkam
Penaadhu azhukkaruppaan.
kurals.meaning: A person who, instead of welcoming another's prosperity, envies it, is effectively someone who wants neither virtue nor prosperity for themselves.
kurals.elementary: If your friend wins a prize and you sulk instead of cheering, you're not just being unkind to them. You're blocking your own chance to be good and to do well. Being jealous is like saying “I don't want good things for myself either.”
kurals.university: The couplet makes a psychological claim: envy is self-defeating, not just unkind. Parimelazhagar reads அறனாக்கம் as both அறம் (virtue) and ஆக்கம் (prosperity). The envious person's attitude implicitly rejects both, since virtue grows through goodwill and prosperity through good conduct. பேணாது (“without cherishing”) implies the right response to another's good fortune is active appreciation, close to the Buddhist mudita (sympathetic joy). Aristotle's definition fits closely: the envious man “is pained at all good fortune,” even when it is deserved.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At Yudhishthira's Rajasuya sacrifice, Duryodhana sees the Pandavas' wealth and splendour and is consumed with jealousy. He tells his father he cannot bear their prosperity, which leads to the rigged dice game.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana cannot welcome his cousins' success and turns to deceit, abandoning dharma for envy.
hinduism.tie_back: He becomes the Kural's envious man exactly: by resenting another's prosperity he gives up both righteousness and, in the end, his own fortune.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), Ganguli translation
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; strong thematic match. Exact section numbers vary across editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to share in others' joy rather than resent it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of cherishing (பேணுதல்) another's prosperity is what Paul commands here.
christianity._accuracy_note: Positive counterpart of the Kural's warning; Paul does not state the self-harm consequence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Or do they envy people for what Allāh has given them of His bounty?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes those who resent the favor God has given to others.
islam.tie_back: Both texts condemn resentment of another's blessing, which in the Qur'anic frame means resenting God's own gift.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct condemnation of envy at others' bounty; the self-defeating aspect is implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.”
judaism.explanation: The tenth commandment forbids even the inner wanting of what belongs to one's neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts target the inner reaction to another's prosperity, not just outward acts.
judaism._accuracy_note: Coveting (wanting it for oneself) overlaps with, but is not identical to, envy (resenting that another has it).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should not despise what one has received, nor envy the gains of others. The monk who envies the gains of others does not attain to meditative absorption.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that envying others' gains blocks one's own spiritual progress.
buddhism.tie_back: Close to the Kural: envying another's prosperity costs the envier his own highest good.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: envy of others' gain directly forfeits one's own spiritual attainment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aglauros, daughter of Cecrops, is filled with envy by the goddess Envy (Invidia) at her sister Herse's good fortune in being loved by Mercury. She wastes away and blocks the god at her sister's door.
greek_mythology.explanation: Instead of rejoicing in her sister's blessing, Aglauros is eaten up by resentment and tries to stop it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She shows the Kural's point: resenting another's prosperity ruins the resenter's own life.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase verified against the Kline translation; strong thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man who is characterized by righteous indignation is pained at undeserved good fortune, the envious man, going beyond him, is pained at all good fortune.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle separates indignation at undeserved success from envy, which resents any success at all, including deserved success.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's envier resents the prosperity of others whatever its source; Aristotle defines envy the same way.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on MIT Internet Classics Archive. Precise conceptual definition; Aristotle does not argue the self-harm point here.

kurals.tamil:
அழுக்காற்றின் அல்லவை செய்யார் இழுக்காற்றின்
ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhukkaatrin allavai seyyaar izhukkaatrin
Edham padupaakku arindhu.
kurals.meaning: The wise, knowing the suffering that comes from walking a wrong path, will not do wrong because of envy.
kurals.elementary: If you know a path has a big muddy pit, you don't walk that way. Wise people know jealousy leads to doing mean things, and mean things lead to trouble, so they don't let jealousy push them into it.
kurals.university: The subject, “the wise” (அறிவுடையோர்), is understood from context, as the commentators note. The couplet treats restraint from envy-driven wrongdoing as a matter of knowledge: seeing where the “fault-path” (இழுக்காறு) leads. Valluvar moves from the feeling of envy (azhukkaaru) to the acts it produces (அல்லவை, unrighteous deeds), and the wise stop the chain at the first link. The reasoning is prudential as well as moral, like the Buddha's image of the trader who avoids a dangerous road. It also matches Aristotle's claim that envy, like theft or murder, has no right amount or right occasion; it is always a mistake.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But those who, out of envy, disregard these teachings and do not practice them regularly, are to be considered bereft of all knowledge, befooled, and doomed to ignorance and bondage.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says those who act out of envy (abhyasūyantaḥ) lose their knowledge and are ruined.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts link envy-driven conduct to a lack of wisdom and its ruinous result.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Envy (asūyā) is explicit in the Sanskrit; the Gita speaks of envy toward the teaching, a narrower object.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that envy is the soil in which every kind of wrongdoing grows.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's chain from envy to wrongful acts appears here: where envy is, “every evil work” follows.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on envy as the source of wrong deeds; James does not frame restraint as the wise person's foresight.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not wish for that by which Allāh has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allāh of His bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids longing for others' advantages and redirects the heart to asking God directly.
islam.tie_back: Both texts stop envy early, before it grows into wrongful acts, by pointing to a better path.
islam._accuracy_note: Prohibits envious longing but does not describe envy-driven deeds or their harm.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.”
judaism.explanation: God warns Cain, angry that Abel's offering was accepted, that sin is waiting at the door and that he must master it before he acts.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's wise person does what Cain failed to do: sees where envy leads and refuses to act on it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Cain's envy is implied by the narrative rather than named; a strong illustration of envy leading to wrongdoing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a trader with a small escort and great wealth would avoid a perilous route, or just as one desiring to live avoids poison, even so should one shun evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a wise person avoiding evil to a trader who knows a road is dangerous and takes another.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's wise avoid the envy-path because they know the danger on it; the Dhammapada uses the same logic.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on the prudential logic; the verse concerns evil generally, not envy specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod warns that the bad Strife “fosters evil war and battle, being cruel: her no man loves,” unlike the good Strife of honest rivalry.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet tells his brother Perses to recognize the destructive form of rivalry and turn away from it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's wise, Hesiod's listener must see where destructive rivalry leads and refuse to follow it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase framing a short verbatim phrase. Hesiod's bad Strife is broader than envy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Some have names that already imply badness, e.g. spite, shamelessness, envy, and in the case of actions adultery, theft, murder ... It is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them; one must always be wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says envy, unlike anger or fear, has no right amount; it is always wrong, just as theft or murder is.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why the Kural's wise never act from envy: there is no case in which envy-driven action is right.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on MIT Internet Classics Archive (ellipsis marks omitted text). Strong on envy always being wrong, less on the foresight theme.

kurals.tamil:
அழுக்காறு உடையார்க்கு அதுசாலும் ஒன்னார்
வழுக்காயும் கேடீன் பது.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaarkku adhusaalum onnaar
Vazhukkaayum kedeenbadhu.
kurals.meaning: For the envious, envy alone is enough. Even if their enemies fail to harm them, envy itself will bring about their ruin.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who never needs a bully to hurt them, because they keep hurting themselves by feeling jealous all the time. Envy is like a bully that lives inside you.
kurals.university: The phrase அது சாலும் (“that is enough”) makes envy a self-sufficient engine of destruction. No external enemy (ஒன்னார்) is needed, and even if enemies falter (வழுக்காயும்), envy does not. The same insight appears across traditions: Proverbs calls envy “the rottenness of the bones,” Ovid pictures Envy gnawing herself, and the Dhammapada compares the depraved man to a creeper that strangles its own host tree. Aristotle's definition explains why: envy is pain at another's good that brings the envier no gain, only suffering.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “These six are always miserable, viz., the envious, the malicious, the discontented, the irascible, the ever-suspicious, and those depending upon the fortunes of others.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that the envious come first among those who are always unhappy, whatever their outward circumstances.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say envy produces its own misery; the envious need no enemy.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), Ganguli translation
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com. Strong match on envy as self-generated misery.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says envy rots a person from the inside, while a calm heart gives life.
christianity.tie_back: Envy destroys from within, needing no enemy, just as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct match: envy as an internal, self-destroying force.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avoid envy, for envy devours good deeds just as fire devours fuel or (he said) “grass.””
islam.explanation: The hadith says envy consumes a person's own store of good deeds, as fire eats up wood.
islam.tie_back: Both texts describe envy as a self-consuming fire that destroys the envier.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match, but graded Da'if (weak) by al-Albani per Sunnah.com. Cited for its wide circulation; its authenticity is disputed.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names envy (kin'ah) first among three passions that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats envy as enough on its own to ruin someone.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match: envy as self-sufficient cause of ruin.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a single creeper strangles the tree on which it grows, even so, a man who is exceedingly depraved harms himself as only an enemy might wish.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a corrupt person to a tree choked by a creeper growing on it: he does to himself what an enemy would want to do.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's point that the envious need no enemy because they are their own.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking structural parallel (self-harm exceeding an enemy's), but the verse addresses depravity generally, not envy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “She finds men's successes disagreeable, and pines away at the sight. She gnaws and being gnawed is also her own punishment.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid personifies Envy (Invidia) as a figure who eats vipers' flesh and wastes away at others' success: she is her own torment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ovid pictures exactly what the Kural states: envy punishes the envier without any outside enemy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified on poetryintranslation.com. Near one-to-one match of image and idea.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Envy is pain at the sight of such good fortune as consists of the good things already mentioned; we feel it towards our equals; not with the idea of getting something for ourselves, but because the other people have it.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines envy as pain at another's good that brings no gain to the envier.
philosophy.tie_back: If envy is pain with no gain, it harms only the envier, which is why the Kural calls it “enough” to ruin a person.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified. The self-harm conclusion follows from the definition but Aristotle does not state it here.

kurals.tamil:
கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான் சுற்றம் உடுப்பதூஉம்
உண்பதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Koduppadhu azhukkaruppaan sutram uduppadhoovum
Unbadhoovum indrik kedum.
kurals.meaning: One who is envious of what is given to others will perish, along with his kin, without even clothing to wear or food to eat.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who gets upset every time a teacher gives stickers to others. Eventually, nobody wants to share with that kid or their friends either. Being jealous of other people's gifts leaves you, and the people around you, with nothing.
kurals.university: This couplet narrows envy to a specific form: resentment of generosity itself (கொடுப்பது, “what is given”), whether one objects to a gift going to someone else or tries to stop it. The punishment is social and material: not only the envier but his சுற்றம் (kin, dependents) are left without food or clothing, since the grudging spirit cuts the household off from the web of mutual giving. The idea has a close counterpart in the Buddha's teaching that whoever obstructs another's gift harms three parties, beginning with himself. Pirkei Avot likewise names the giver who wishes others would not give as having an “evil eye” toward what belongs to others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When King Bali prepares to grant three steps of land to the dwarf Vamana, his preceptor Shukracharya urges him to withhold the gift. Bali refuses, gives anyway, and is ultimately blessed; later retellings add that Shukra lost an eye trying to block the gift.
hinduism.explanation: Shukra tries to stop a gift from being given, and his obstruction fails.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural condemns the one who resents or blocks another's giving; Shukra's attempt is a well-known illustration of that failure.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial match. Shukra's motive in the Bhagavata is protective caution rather than envy, and the lost-eye detail comes from later/popular retellings, not the Bhagavata text itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the vineyard workers, the owner answers those who resent his generosity to latecomers: are they envious (“evil eye”) because he is generous?
christianity.tie_back: Jesus confronts exactly the envy the Kural condemns: resenting what is given to someone else.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on the object of envy (another's gift). The Kural's consequence (destitution) is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who are stingy and enjoin upon [other] people stinginess and conceal what Allāh has given them of His bounty - and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment -”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns those who are stingy themselves and also urge others not to give.
islam.tie_back: Both texts condemn those who obstruct others' generosity and warn of humiliating loss.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on obstructing generosity; envy is not named explicitly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are four types of charity givers. He who wishes to give, but that others should not give: his eye is evil to that which belongs to others.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah singles out the person who resents others' giving as having an “evil eye” toward what belongs to them.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact target: resentment of what others give.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on the object of the vice; Avot does not state the consequence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates three obstructions, three impediments. Which three? He creates an obstruction to the merit of the giver, an obstruction to the recipient's gains, and prior to that he undermines and harms his own self.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Vacchagotta that blocking someone else's gift harms the giver, the receiver, and, first of all, the one who blocks it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts teach that begrudging another's giving ends in the begrudger's own ruin.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.57 (Vaccha Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight. Near one-to-one match of vice and consequence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Envy travels to Athens, “wherever she passes she tramples the flower-filled fields, withers the grass, blasts the highest treetops and poisons homes, cities and peoples with her breath.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's Envy does not stay inside one heart; her breath blights crops and poisons whole communities.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, where the envier's kin lose food and clothing, envy's damage spreads to the people around the envier.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified wording. The link is thematic (envy's damage spreading to others) rather than about resenting gifts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Emulation makes us take steps to secure the good things in question, envy makes us take steps to stop our neighbour having them.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notes that envy is active: it moves people to stop others from getting good things.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's envier who resents what is given to others is Aristotle's envious man trying to stop his neighbour from receiving.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified. Strong match on the obstructive nature of envy; no statement of consequences.

kurals.tamil:
அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு உடையானைச் செய்யவள்
தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Avvithu azhukkaaru udaiyaanaich cheyyaval
Thavvaiyaik kaatti vidum.
kurals.meaning: The goddess of fortune (Lakshmi, “the red one”), resenting the envious man, leaves him and points him out to her elder sister, the goddess of misfortune.
kurals.elementary: Imagine Good Luck as a friendly person who visits your house. When she sees you're always jealous, she leaves, and on her way out she tells her grumpy sister, Bad Luck, “This house is yours now.”
kurals.university: Valluvar here uses a mythological image unusual for a text that mostly avoids sectarian deities. செய்யவள் (“the red/fair one”) is Lakshmi (Tiru), and தவ்வை (“elder sister”) is Mudevi/Jyeshtha, goddess of misfortune, who in the Padma and Linga Puranas rises from the churned ocean before Lakshmi and is told to dwell among the quarrelsome and wicked. அவ்வித்து is read by Parimelazhagar as “being herself envious [of him],” so the goddess answers envy with envy, a measure-for-measure punishment. The image turns an abstract claim, that envy drives away prosperity, into a vivid scene, a technique Valluvar uses sparingly and to strong effect.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Jyeshtha (Mudevi), elder sister and opposite of Lakshmi, emerges from the churning of the ocean before Lakshmi; in the Padma and Linga Puranas she is told to dwell in homes of quarrel, harsh speech, and wicked people.
hinduism.explanation: Hindu myth pairs prosperity (Lakshmi) with her elder sister misfortune (Jyeshtha), who takes over where vice lives.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses this exact pair: Lakshmi leaves the envious man and hands him over to her elder sister.
hinduism.source: Padma Purana and Linga Purana, as summarized in the Wikipedia article on Jyestha (citing Leslie 1992 and Kinsley 1997)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match: the Kural itself references this mythological pair. Summary via a secondary web source citing academic works.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that the grasping, “evil-eyed” person does not see that poverty is coming for him.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the envious “evil eye” drives prosperity away and invites poverty.
christianity._accuracy_note: “Evil eye” in Hebrew idiom connotes envy/stinginess; no personified goddesses.

islam.quote_or_event: Iblis refuses to bow to Adam, saying “I am better than him,” and is told: “Descend from it [i.e., Paradise]... So get out; indeed, you are of the debased.”
islam.explanation: Iblis resents the honor given to Adam and is expelled from the place of favor.
islam.tie_back: As Lakshmi abandons the envious man, divine favor is withdrawn from Iblis because he resented another's elevation.
islam._accuracy_note: The Qur'anic text names arrogance; classical exegesis also reads Iblis's refusal as envy (hasad) of Adam. Partial match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” ... “And Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him, and was departed from Saul.”
judaism.explanation: After hearing David praised above him, Saul watches him with an envious eye, and the text notes that God's presence has left Saul and gone to David.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the envious man is abandoned by divine favor, which passes to the one he envies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel of favor departing from the envier.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where a woman or man is envious. He/she envies, begrudges, & broods about others' gains, honor, respect, reverence, salutations, & veneration. ... If instead he/she comes to the human state, then he/she is not influential wherever reborn.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that envy leads to rebirth in bad destinations or, if reborn human, to a life without influence or standing.
buddhism.tie_back: Envy drives good fortune away, which is the Kural's point in karmic rather than mythological terms.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 135 (Cula-kammavibhanga Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; ellipsis marks omitted text. Same cause-and-effect, without personified deities.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod's iron age, “Envy, foul-mouthed, delighting in evil, with scowling face, will go along with wretched men one and all. And then Aidos and Nemesis ... will go from the wide-pathed earth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Envy becomes people's companion, the goddesses of shame and righteous retribution leave the earth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As Lakshmi leaves the envious man, Hesiod's good goddesses abandon a humanity that keeps company with Envy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; ellipsis marks omitted text. Strong image of goddesses departing when envy arrives.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For jealousy has no place in the celestial choir.”
philosophy.explanation: In Socrates' myth of the soul's journey, the gods move freely through heaven and anyone able may follow, because envy has no place among the divine.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato puts envy outside the divine company; the Kural shows the goddess of fortune leaving the envious.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on MIT Internet Classics Archive. Thematic link (the divine excludes envy); not about fortune leaving an individual.

kurals.tamil:
அழுக்காறு எனஒரு பாவி திருச்செற்றுத்
தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhukkaaru ena oru paavi thiruchchetruth
Theeyuzhi uyththu vidum.
kurals.meaning: Envy, a sinner without equal, destroys a person's wealth and drives him onto the path of evil, even into the fire of hell.
kurals.elementary: Envy is like a sneaky thief who first steals everything you have, then pushes you onto a dangerous road. Once envy moves in, it takes your good things away and leads you somewhere bad.
kurals.university: Valluvar personifies envy as a பாவி (sinner, evil being) with no equal (ஒரு), and gives it two acts: it destroys wealth (திருச்செற்று, with திரு again evoking Lakshmi from the previous couplet) and drives its host into தீயுழி. The term means “evil place” or “evil path”; Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as hell, others as a life of wrongdoing. The double sense covers both this-worldly ruin and afterlife punishment, a pattern also seen in the Dhammapada's “suffers here and hereafter.” Parallels such as Korah and Devadatta, whose envy ended with the earth swallowing them, show how widely traditions have linked envy to a downward plunge.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are envious and mischievous, who are the lowest among men, I perpetually cast into the ocean of material existence, into various demoniac species of life.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the envious (dviṣataḥ) and cruel are repeatedly cast into lower, demonic births.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say envy drives a person downward to the worst destination.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on Vedabase. Dviṣataḥ is more often rendered “hateful”; the envy reading is Prabhupada's.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one.”
christianity.explanation: Eliphaz tells Job that envy kills the simple person who harbors it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's “sinner without equal,” envy is pictured as a killer of its host.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on envy's destructiveness; the specific themes of lost wealth and hell are absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “And his soul permitted to him the murder of his brother, so he killed him and became among the losers.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells of Adam's son who, after his brother's offering was accepted and his was not, killed him and became “among the losers.”
islam.tie_back: Envy of a brother's acceptance leads to the gravest sin and lasting loss, the path the Kural describes.
islam._accuracy_note: The Qur'an narrates the killing after the accepted offering; the envy motive is drawn from context and exegesis rather than named.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They, and all that appertained to them, went down alive into the pit, and the earth closed upon them: and they perished from among the congregation.”
judaism.explanation: Korah and his followers, who challenged Moses and Aaron out of jealousy of their position, are swallowed by the earth with all their possessions.
judaism.tie_back: Envy destroys wealth (“all that appertained to them”) and plunges the envier into the pit, as in the Kural.
judaism.source: Numbers 16:33 (KJV); cf. Pirkei Avot 5:17 on Korah's dispute
judaism._accuracy_note: Korah's envy is the standard rabbinic reading of Numbers 16; the verse itself describes the punishment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The evil-doer suffers here and hereafter; he suffers in both the worlds. The thought, “Evil have I done,” torments him, and he suffers even more when gone to realms of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial tradition attaches this verse to Devadatta, whose envy of the Buddha led to schism and assassination attempts, and who was swallowed by the earth into hell.
buddhism.tie_back: Envy ruins in this life and drives to hell hereafter, the two-stage fall the Kural describes.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 17 (trans. Buddharakkhita); Devadatta story from the Dhammapada Commentary
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verse verified; the Devadatta link comes from the commentary, not the verse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aglauros, poisoned by Envy, blocks Mercury from reaching her sister; the god turns her into a dark stone statue, stained by her envious mind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy destroys Aglauros's life and fortune completely, ending in her punishment by a god.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's “sinner,” Envy wrecks its host and delivers her to a terrible end.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; strong match on ruin but not on an afterlife hell.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle groups envy with spite and shamelessness, and with adultery, theft, and murder, as things that “imply by their names that they are themselves bad”; for all of them, “one must always be wrong.”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, envy is not a feeling to moderate but a vice that always leads a person wrong.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's “sinner without equal” and Aristotle's “always wrong” both treat envy as corrupt at its root.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase with short verbatim phrases. Partial match on envy as inherently evil; nothing on lost wealth or hell.

kurals.tamil:
அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான்
கேடும் நினைக்கப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Avviya nenjathaan aakkamum sevviyaan
Kedum ninaikkap padum.
kurals.meaning: The prosperity of a person with an envious heart, and the misfortune of an upright one, are things that must be pondered, for they are anomalies that call for explanation.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a mean, jealous kid seems to get everything, while a kind kid has a hard time. That looks unfair, and this kural says: stop and think about it. Things may not stay that way, and there is a deeper reason behind it.
kurals.university: Valluvar recognizes the classic problem of theodicy: the wicked sometimes prosper and the good sometimes suffer. He does not deny it. He calls these cases நினைக்கப்படும், “to be reflected upon.” Parimelazhagar resolves the anomaly through karma: the envious man's prosperity comes from past merit now being used up, and the good man's suffering from past deeds now being paid off, so neither lasts. The same wrestling appears in Psalm 73, in Rabbi Yannai's admission in Pirkei Avot, in the Dhammapada's teaching that evil “ripens” late, and in Glaucon's challenge in Plato's Republic, which makes this one of the most widely shared questions in world ethics.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In exile in the forest, Draupadi laments to Yudhishthira that the righteous king suffers while the wicked Duryodhana prospers, and questions divine justice; Yudhishthira answers that one practices dharma for its own sake and that its fruits come in time.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata stages a full debate over why the virtuous suffer and the envious thrive.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the anomaly the Kural says must be pondered: the envious prosper and the upright suffer.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Draupadi–Yudhishthira dialogue), Ganguli translation
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. Duryodhana's envy is central to the epic; section numbering varies by edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. ... Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist is troubled that the wicked prosper, until reflection in God's sanctuary shows him their final end.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: the prosperity of the wicked is a puzzle to be pondered until one sees how it ends.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified; near one-to-one match on the anomaly and the call to reflect.

islam.quote_or_event: “And let not those who disbelieve ever think that [because] We extend their time [of enjoyment] it is better for them. We only extend it for them so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an explains that the apparent prosperity of wrongdoers is a respite that will end in punishment, not a sign of favor.
islam.tie_back: Both texts ask the reader to think past the surface when the undeserving prosper.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the prosperity of the undeserving; the suffering of the righteous is addressed elsewhere.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Yannai said: it is not in our hands [to explain the reason] either of the security of the wicked, or even of the afflictions of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah admits that the ease of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous are beyond full human explanation.
judaism.tie_back: It names the same two anomalies as the Kural: the wicked's prosperity and the upright's suffering.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-exact structural match: both halves of the anomaly appear together.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It may be well with the evil-doer as long as the evil ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the evil-doer sees (the painful results of) his evil deeds. It may be ill with the doer of good as long as the good ripens not. But when it does ripen, then the doer of good sees (the pleasant results of) his good deeds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha explains that results of deeds ripen with a delay, so the wicked may prosper and the good suffer for a while.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the karmic resolution that Parimelazhagar gives for the Kural's anomaly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; very close match on both halves plus the resolving principle.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the wealthy King Croesus asks Solon who is the happiest of men, Solon refuses to call Croesus happy and says no one should be called fortunate until one has seen how his life ends; Croesus later loses his kingdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: Solon warns that visible prosperity is no sure sign of lasting fortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story invites reflection on why fortune seems to go to the wrong people, and on how it ends.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong on reflecting about fortune; Croesus is not portrayed as envious.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Book II of the Republic, Glaucon challenges Socrates with the case of the perfectly unjust man who enjoys wealth and reputation and the perfectly just man who is thought unjust and suffers torture. Socrates spends the rest of the dialogue showing that justice is still better.
philosophy.explanation: Plato builds his central ethical argument around the anomaly of the prosperous wicked and the suffering righteous.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same anomaly must be pondered; the Republic ponders it at length.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong structural match; envy is not specifically named.

kurals.tamil:
அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை அஃதுஇல்லார்
பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhukkatru akandraarum illai aqdhuillaar
Perukkaththil theerndhaarum il.
kurals.meaning: No one has ever risen to greatness through envy, and no one free from envy has ever fallen away from prosperity.
kurals.elementary: Being jealous has never helped anyone become great, not even once. And people who are happy for others never end up losing out because of it. So jealousy has zero upside, and kindness has zero downside.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a balanced pair of universal negatives: அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை (none have grown great through envy; அகன்றார், literally “expanded”) and அஃதில்லார் பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல் (none without it have been cut off from increase). The form is a complete disjunction: envy never helps and its absence never hurts, so envy is irrational even on purely selfish grounds. Read with Kural 169, the couplet resolves the anomaly: apparent exceptions are temporary and the long-run pattern holds. The prudential argument matches Epictetus: if someone gains an advantage by paying a price you did not pay, “don't imagine that he has gained any advantage over you.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana, whose envy of the Pandavas drives the whole conflict, dies at Kurukshetra with his brothers and allies destroyed, while the Pandavas, whom he tried to ruin, recover the kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: The epic's overall arc shows the envious prince losing everything and his envied cousins restored.
hinduism.tie_back: Its conclusion matches the Kural's: envy raised no one, and those it targeted did not ultimately fall.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata (overall narrative; Shalya and Sauptika Parvas), Ganguli translation
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. The Pandavas' own righteousness is complex, and their victory costs them dearly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the prodigal son, the father answers the elder brother, who resents the feast for his returned brother, that he has lost nothing.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural says the unenvious never lose prosperity; the father tells the envious son he never lacked anything to begin with.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial match: shows envy gains nothing, but the parable's focus is grace and reconciliation.

islam.quote_or_event: People envy Qarun's great wealth, saying “Oh, would that we had like what was given to Qārūn.” After the earth swallows him, the same people say, “Oh, how Allāh extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it!”
islam.explanation: Those who envied Qarun's riches realize, after his destruction, that envying him would have brought them nothing but ruin.
islam.tie_back: The story teaches the Kural's lesson: envied prosperity was not real greatness, and envy leads nowhere.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified wording of the key clauses; the story shows the emptiness of envied wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.”
judaism.explanation: Joseph's brothers envy him and sell him into slavery, yet Joseph rises to rule Egypt and they end up bowing before him.
judaism.tie_back: The envious brothers gained nothing by their envy, and the envied Joseph was not held down, as the Kural says.
judaism.source: Genesis 37:11 (KJV), with the narrative of Genesis 37-45
judaism._accuracy_note: Verse verified; the rise-and-fall pattern comes from the wider narrative.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where a woman or man is not envious. He/she does not envy, begrudge, or brood about others' gains, honor, respect, reverence, salutations, or veneration. ... he/she is influential wherever reborn.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that freedom from envy leads to good rebirth and to influence and standing in future lives.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the second half of the Kural: those free from envy never fall from greatness.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 135 (Cula-kammavibhanga Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified; ellipsis marks omitted text. Close match on the envy-to-standing link.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the good Strife, under which a man seeing a rich neighbour works harder to plough, plant, and set his own house in order, and says “This Strife is wholesome for men,” unlike the destructive kind.
greek_mythology.explanation: Honest emulation, which works to match a neighbour's success rather than resent it, is what makes people prosper.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, prosperity comes to those without envy, not to the envious.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase with verified phrases. Hesiod's emulation is competitive, so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If another, then, paying fifty cents, takes the lettuce, and you, not paying it, go without them, don't imagine that he has gained any advantage over you. For as he has the lettuce, so you have the fifty cents which you did not give.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus argues that someone else's gain is never really your loss, so envy has no reason to exist.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers argue that envy never helps, and that one who does not envy loses nothing.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified on MIT Internet Classics Archive. Strong on the pointlessness of envy.

ytamizh-ch17.title: Thirukkural Chapter 17: அழுக்காறாமை / Not Envying (with Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar commentaries and Drew/Lazarus English)

aristotle-rhetoric.title: Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book II, trans. W. Rhys Roberts

aristotle-nicomachean.title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, trans. W. D. Ross

ovid-met-invidia.title: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book II (Aglauros and Envy, II:708-832), trans. A. S. Kline

hesiod-works-days.title: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914)

herodotus-histories.title: Herodotus, The Histories, Book 1 (Solon and Croesus), trans. A. D. Godley

mahabharata-udyoga-33.title: The Mahabharata, Book 5: Udyoga Parva, Section XXXIII (Vidura Niti), trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli

mahabharata-ganguli.title: The Mahabharata, trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

bhagavata-purana.title: Srimad Bhagavatam, Canto 8, Chapters 19-20 (Vamana and Bali), trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada
